deposits.notes:
Replication Data for: Designing Human and Generative AI Collaboration; Harvard Dataverse version 1.0. Metadata lists deposit date 2024-11-20 and publication 2024-11-21. Found in the paper, repeated in both form URL fields, and independently retrieved by title search. The DOI request returned HTTP 202 with an empty body after redirecting to https://dataverse.harvard.edu/citation?persistentId=doi:10.7910/DVN/ATXBCK; http_status records that observed response. The dataset API https://dataverse.harvard.edu/api/datasets/:persistentId/?persistentId=doi:10.7910/DVN/ATXBCK returned HTTP 200 and listed 29 files, all restricted=false. Public access was independently confirmed by HTTP 200 downloads through https://dataverse.harvard.edu/api/access/datafile/<id>.

rows_checked and columns_checked describe Replication Data for Designing Human and Generative AI Collaboration.csv (file ID 10719127): 2,196 evaluation rows, 549 distinct participant-day stories, exactly four rows per story, and 285 distinct participant IDs. unique_id equals ID + '_' + Day. Every ID has one stable Group; Day is 1 or 2. Originality, Interestingness, Writing, Coherence, and Overall have no missing entries. Evaluator and external permit inspection of rater dependence; the raw evaluator identifiers should be checked before modeling shared raters (three duplicate story/Evaluator pairs were observed). Participant characteristics and survey outcomes are repeated across rating rows, so they must be aggregated or deduplicated before analysis.

Counts observed in the ratings file, not inferred from the PDF: across either day, Human Confirmation 95 IDs, Human Creativity 99, Copilot 91 (285 total). Day 1: 93, 96, and 89 respectively (278 stories). Day 2: 88, 93, and 90 respectively (271 stories). There are 264 IDs on both days, 14 only on Day 1, and 7 only on Day 2. Grouping by ID gives 280 IDs with all four baseline covariates (DAT, Ability, Experience, English). With those covariates complete, person counts by Human Confirmation/Human Creativity/Copilot are 90/95/89 on Day 1 and 85/92/90 on Day 2. These identify outcome and complete-case samples; no separate randomization/withdrawal ledger establishes counts of all randomized students.

Raw texts and nine binary genre indicators were read in four files: genre_Confirmation.csv (10719121), 91 rows; genre_Copilot.csv (10719140), 91; genre_Creativity.csv (10719118), 93; genre_day1.csv (10719131), 282. Their columns are Unnamed: 0, Story, Prior Genre, Top 3 Genres, Horror Fiction, Mystery/Crime Fiction, Romance, Sci-Fi, Thriller/Suspense, Western Fiction, Historical Fiction, Young Adult Fiction, Fantasy. Story is nonempty and unique within each file; the nine genre columns are complete and binary. Assigned condition is established by filenames and the diversity notebook, not a participant-ID column. Unnamed: 0 is only a separate zero-based sequence in each file. No documented crosswalk to ID/unique_id in the ratings file was found. Thus the 557 text rows (282 baseline and 275 AI-assisted) cannot be assumed to be the same 549 rated stories (278 and 271). In particular, text counts for Human Confirmation and Copilot exceed rated Day 2 story counts.

Embedding files 3large_result_df_A.csv (10719133; Human Creativity), 3large_result_df_B.csv (10719117; Human Confirmation), and 3large_result_df_C.csv (10719128; Copilot) were read: 93, 91, and 91 rows respectively. Each has Unnamed: 0, Story, Embedding, Similarity. Parsed embeddings have 3,072 dimensions; texts match the corresponding genre file in order. They likewise lack participant identifiers. 3large_result_df_Day1.csv is listed as 21,032,094 bytes, above the 20 MB limit, and was not downloaded or assigned a confirmed row count. Baseline story texts are available in the smaller genre_day1.csv. In the three inspected embedding files, stored Similarity values did not exactly match cosine similarity to the mean of the other listed embeddings; the inspected notebooks load the scores rather than document their construction.

All six Jupyter notebooks were downloaded as JSON and inspected without executing them. Fig. 2. Effects on overall story quality.ipynb (10719132) and Supplementary Material.ipynb (10719129), including zero-based cells 19-22 for Table S7, use ordinary statsmodels OLS .fit() without a clustered/robust covariance option or evaluator terms for the relevant rating regressions. The code also shows aggregation by ID for the participant-level inequality analysis. Table 1. Descriptive statistics.ipynb (10719114) explicitly groups participant characteristics by ID and survey outcomes by ID/Day.

Fig. 4. Treatment effects on content diversity.ipynb (10719142), zero-based cell 4, computes genre similarities for every unordered pair of stories and forms t intervals using stats.sem over those pairwise values; it does not resample stories or adjust the interval for overlapping pairs. This differs from the PDF p. 16 caption's story-versus-average-of-other-stories formula. Cell 8 forms t intervals from the stored per-story semantic Similarity column. The code establishes the posted procedures, but does not resolve the genre-method discrepancy or the construction of semantic scores. No explicit significance-test code for the claimed diversity differences was identified.

studies_covered identifies the randomized writing study S1. Human baseline DAT scores also cover the human side of ancillary S2, but no separate raw ten-word DAT responses or 20 autonomous ChatGPT DAT scores/outputs were identified. Reflections, full ChatGPT conversations, a participant-to-text crosswalk, and a randomization roster were not identified in the complete file listing. License is the dataset API's CC0 1.0.

what_we_could_compute: For S1-O1 through S1-O5, average the four ratings within ID/Day to obtain one score per participant per day; compute arm-specific means, participant-level SDs, SEs, analyzed Ns, and all randomized Day 2 arm contrasts. The matched IDs also permit paired Day 1/Day 2 analyses, retaining the form's warning that day/order was not randomized.

For final.open_items open_questions[0] and the unresolved S1 analyzed-person total, reconstruct exact outcome-sample counts and overlap by arm/day and counts with the covariates required by the posted regressions. The observed unique analyzed-person count is 285. The data also reproduce 280 IDs with baseline covariates and 278/271 rated stories. Counts of all randomized participants, including anyone with no included outcome, and reasons for nonresponse require a separate assignment/flow record.

For open_questions[1], identify the posted OLS variance specification and fit independent participant-level analyses or participant-clustered rating analyses. The Evaluator field allows investigation of shared-rater dependence after validating the raw identifiers. The code and data supply the necessary information to calculate precision without treating four ratings of one story as four independent people.

For open_questions[2] and S1-O6 through S1-O9, compute genre counts/composition and both pairwise and story-versus-centroid diversity measures from the deposited story texts and binary genre vectors; recompute semantic measures using the inspected Day 2 embeddings or new embeddings of the public texts. SDs and resampling-based uncertainty can be computed for the deposited story pools. The posted notebook reveals its t-interval formulas and the genre-method mismatch. Participant-linked or paired-across-day text analyses, reconciliation with the 549-story ratings sample, and verification of the original semantic-score construction still need a participant-to-text crosswalk or author clarification.

Public files do not settle open_questions[3] (75 versus 105 minutes), open_questions[4] (exact saved manuscript revision), or the Atlas vocabulary choice in open_questions[5]. S2 can be summarized on the human DAT side only; the autonomous AI benchmark data were not identified.
notes:
Checked on 2026-10-10 using unauthenticated Python urllib requests with User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1. Read the complete 1,210-line markdown conversion, including all Supporting Information through PDF p. 57; repeated identical cells in malformed markdown tables were displayed once with multiplicity. Checked relevant PDF text and every external PDF link annotation. Quotes preserve the source wording, with whitespace and line breaks normalized; the page number interrupting the cross-page quotation was removed.

The paper and both form data_and_code fields identify the same Dataverse DOI, counted once. No preregistration statement or registry link was found. The MDAR Reproducibility Checklist is listed on PDF p. 17 but is absent from the saved PDF and the repository file list. Instructions refer to a Google Spreadsheet, Google Document template, and class prompt guidelines, but neither the markdown nor PDF link annotations provides URLs for them; these are unlocated materials, not verified restricted deposits.

Other paper links checked: https://www.datcreativity.com/ (PDF p. 35, DAT instrument) HTTP 200; https://jerichowriters.com/types-of-novels/ (PDF p. 10, reference 26) HTTP 200; https://jakobnielsenphd.substack.com/p/ideation-is-free-ai-strong-creativity (PDF p. 57, SI reference 2) HTTP 200. These are an instrument and background references, not deposits of this study's data. Email links were not followed and no authors were contacted.

The supplied article landing page https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.14199 returned HTTP 200. It identifies v2, revised 29 January 2025, and says the manuscript includes Supplementary Information. No journal reference or separate supplementary-data download was identified there, so no journal publisher landing URL could be confirmed. This does not identify the exact revision of the saved undated manuscript.

Title and first-author queries were completed through DataCite, Zenodo, Harvard Dataverse, and the specified OSF title-filter API. Successful results yielded no additional relevant deposit. All attempts, including Zenodo validation errors and a timeout, are recorded in searches; failed requests are not coded as zero results.

Classification is public_participant_data because the public ratings table supplies participant/story identifiers, assigned arm, and all five outcome scores. It is not a claim that every collected record is public or every diversity statistic is fully reproducible. Participant-linked raw text, a randomization roster, collected ChatGPT histories/reflection essays, and the autonomous ChatGPT DAT benchmark records were not identified in the listed files. All inspected downloads were read in memory; no data files were saved. No account, login, access request, CAPTCHA interaction, or bot-check bypass was used.
